data.raw_text:
This is one of the oldest recipes in human history. It is literally rice boiled with water. That is the whole recipe, and it has been feeding humanity for somewhere between 7,000 and 9,000 years.

Archaeological evidence of rice being cooked into porridge in the Yangtze River Valley dates to around 7000 BC. Not eaten as grains, not roasted, but specifically boiled down into a soft gruel in clay pots. The most natural thing you could do with rice and fire. By the Zhou Dynasty, it was documented in the Book of Rites as part of everyday life, specifically recommended for the elderly and the sick. During the Han Dynasty the physician Zhang Zhongjing, known as Chinese Hippocrates, prescribed it in his medical texts to restore strength and warm the stomach after illness. Buddhist temples served it as a charitable dish to the poor and pilgrims. It became a festival food, a healing food, a first food for babies, a last resort during famine, and a comfort in every circumstance in between.

It also spread across the entire continent. In Japan it became okayu, eaten by people recovering from illness. In Korea it became juk, elaborate versions made with abalone or chicken. In Vietnam it became cháo, served with herbs and fish sauce. In the Philippines it became lugaw, fragrant with ginger and garlic. Same dish, nine thousand years of different interpretations, still being eaten this morning by hundreds of millions of people.
